claims.text: Conventional W–Cu composites can be manufactured by mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing.
The baseline W–Cu composite has poor W–Cu bonding and relatively high interfacial thermal resistance.
The intervention is incorporation of 1–3 wt.% TiC nanoparticles into the initial W–Cu powder mixture.
TiC nanoparticles will segregate preferentially to W–Cu interfaces during fabrication.
Interfacial TiC will form a robust W–TiC–Cu network.
An interfacial carbide phase can enhance bonding between a metal matrix and a dissimilar reinforcement.
TiC will enhance bonding specifically at W–Cu interfaces.
TiC nanoparticles will act as highly conductive bridges across W–Cu interfaces.
The TiC interfacial network will reduce W–Cu interfacial contact resistance.
Interfacial TiC will reduce phonon scattering at W–Cu interfaces.
Interfacial TiC will reduce void formation at W–Cu interfaces.
TiC has sufficient ceramic stability and irradiation tolerance to help preserve the composite's mechanical integrity under fusion-reactor conditions.
Adding 1–3 wt.% TiC will appreciably increase the thermal conductivity of W–Cu relative to an otherwise comparable TiC-free composite.
The TiC-modified composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the TiC-free W–Cu control.
The TiC-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the TiC-free W–Cu control.
The predicted benefit should hold under high thermal flux and neutron or ion irradiation representative of fusion-reactor joint applications.
The beneficial TiC concentration window is approximately 1–3 wt.%.
TiC loadings above the proposed window may cause nanoparticle agglomeration, reduced ductility, or irradiation-associated brittleness.

The hypothesis is falsified if TiC addition fails to produce a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase or causes a concomitant loss of mechanical durability or irradiation resistance relative to the control.
